issues.legal_issue: On an application for permission to sue without payment of court fees, the court determines whether the pleaded allegations, assumed true, disclose a cause of action and does not decide the merits of the claim.
material_facts: A minor applied for permission to sue without payment of court fees, seeking a declaration of title to an estate and related relief.
The application pleaded alternative grounds of succession, including that the estate had devolved through a reversionary heir after the widow’s death.

The lower courts rejected the application after considering whether the pleaded succession claims were legally sustainable, including questions involving the estate’s character and the effect of legislation.
issues.conclusion: The allegations, if accepted as true, disclosed a cause of action; the application could not be rejected by deciding disputed merits or complicated legal questions at the permission stage.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order XXXIII rules 4, 5(d), 6 and 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the court must determine whether the allegations in the application, taken as true, would entitle the applicant to relief. It may not try issues affecting the merits, consider defences on the merits, or undertake an elaborate inquiry into doubtful or complicated questions of law or fact. No earlier cases are relied on.

predicates.pauper_suit_permission_application: A claimant applies to institute a suit without paying the required court fees.
predicates.pleaded_facts_if_true_entitle_claimant_t: The claimant pleads facts which, if accepted as true, would entitle the claimant to the relief sought.

issues.definition: When a claimant applies to sue without paying court fees and the pleaded facts, assumed true, would entitle the claimant to relief, the application shows a cause of action.

issues.legal_issue: A person seeking to be transposed as an applicant in a proceeding to sue without payment of court fees cannot have the request rejected merely because the original applicant’s request is said to be personal; the proposed applicant’s eligibility must be investigated.
material_facts: A father who was already a party to the proposed suit sought to be transposed as an applicant in his minor son’s application to sue without payment of court fees.

The father’s request was rejected on the ground that permission to sue without payment of court fees was personal to the original applicant and that the rule on adding or striking parties did not apply.
The father had not established that he was entitled to proceed without payment of court fees.
issues.conclusion: The request for transposition could not be rejected on the ground that the original applicant’s request was personal. The proposed applicant had to be a pauper, and his claim to join had to be investigated.
issues.legal_principle: An application under Order XXXIII of the Code of Civil Procedure is a method of instituting a suit, and the suit commences when the application is presented. Order I rule 10 therefore applies to that suit as it does to a suit for which court fees have been paid. A person seeking to join as an applicant must himself qualify as a pauper, but the request cannot be rejected merely as personal to the original applicant. No earlier cases are relied on.

predicates.pauper_suit_application_presented: A claimant has presented an application to institute a suit without paying the required court fees.
predicates.existing_party_seeks_transposition: A person already a party to the proposed suit asks to be transposed as an applicant.
predicates.refusal_rests_only_on_personal_nature_of: The court refuses the requested transposition solely because it treats the original applicant’s request to proceed without court fees as personal.

issues.definition: When an application to sue without court fees has been presented, an existing party seeks transposition, and the request is refused solely as personal to the original applicant, the proposed transposition requires inquiry.
